How to use the simulator

1 Quick start · 2 Top bar · 3 Tabs · 4 DCS console · 5 Faceplates · 6 Trends and alarms · 7 SIS · 8 Field · 9 Exercises · 10 Debrief and data export · 11 Symbols and colours

1 · Quick start

  1. Click anywhere once so the browser allows alarm sound. Check the top bar shows 🔔 Sound on.
  2. The session opens at design: boiler feed water (BFW) 100 m³/h heated from 18 °C to 70 °C by flash steam. Open P&ID to see the plant, then DCS console to operate it.
  3. Go to Exercises, pick a list (Training, Think EQUIPPED or Procedures) and click Load. A blue banner gives the situation; click Acknowledge on the banner to hide it.
  4. Operate from the DCS console: click an instrument bubble, a valve or a pump to open its faceplate on the right. Field hand valves (V-101 … V-105) and outside checks are on the Field tab.
  5. Use Speed to run faster (2×–50×) and Freeze to pause while you think. Many problems in this unit develop over hours: use 20× or 50×.
  6. When finished, open Debrief and grading for your score, then Data export to download CSV files for your report.

2 · Top bar

ControlWhat it does
ClockSimulated time since the session or exercise started (hh:mm:ss).
Freeze / RunPauses and resumes the simulation. Nothing changes while frozen, but you can still read and click.
Speed1× to 50× real time. Grading uses simulated time, so speed does not change your score.
Status lampGreen: steam on, with the vent configuration (rev A, B or C). Amber: XV-100 closed. Red: SIS tripped or water hammer. Click it to open the SIS screen.
🔔 Sound on / 🔕 Sound offOne short beep = new alarm; two alternating tones = trip or water hammer. It repeats until acknowledged or silenced.
SilenceStops the sound only. Alarms keep flashing until acknowledged. A new alarm sounds again.
AcknowledgeAcknowledges every alarm in the list. Unacknowledged alarms older than 60 s cost points.
ScoreContinuous score for this session (starts at 100).

3 · Tabs

The tabs are arranged in six groups (top row); the second row shows the tabs of the chosen group, and each group remembers the tab you last opened. P&ID sits under both Process & Design and Operate, Safety layers under both Process & Design and Safety, and SOP under both Operability and Train & Assess: it is the same page in each place. On a phone the second row becomes a drop-down list.

4 · DCS console

  • Overview: all instruments, plus a summary at top left (BFW flow and temperatures, steam and shell pressure, water and steam duty, SIS and vent state).
  • Temperature profile: the BFW temperature along the tubes drawn from TI-103, TT-101 and the saturation temperature of PI-100 (dashed = design), with the NTU worked out from the three temperatures. NTU = ln((Ts − Tin)/(Ts − Tout)) tells you how UA/F compares with design without a flowmeter.
  • Steam and condensate: header, XV-100, FV-104, steam flow, shell pressure and saturation, superheat, and the heat balance: steam × latent heat against water F·cp·ΔT. A balance off by more than 5 % is shown in red.
  • BFW system: pumps, discharge pressure, FV-101A and its recycle FV-101B, flow, inlet temperature and the tube-side ΔP compared with the clean value at the same flow.

Instrument bubbles follow ISA style: letters on top, loop number below, live value underneath, controller mode (MAN, AUTO, CAS) at upper right. A red value is in alarm; a flashing value is not yet acknowledged. A square around a bubble marks a trip switch (FSLL, TSHH, PSHH). There is no level instrument on the shell: to find a condensate level you must go to the field.

5 · Faceplates

PartWhat it does
PV, barsLarge number is the measured value. The PV bar shows it on the range; the tick shows the set point; the OUT bar shows the valve signal.
Manual / Automatic / CascadeManual: you set OUT. Automatic: you set SP. Cascade (FIC-104 only): its set point is the output of TIC-101. While FIC-104 is not in Cascade, TIC-101 output tracks the FIC-104 set point so the switch is bumpless.
SP and OUT fields, − / +Type a value and press Enter, or step it. SP is locked in Cascade; OUT works only in Manual.
TuningGain, reset (s) and rate (s). Changes take effect on Apply and are logged.
Field hand valvesClick V-101 … V-105 on the drawing: buttons 0, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100 % open.
PumpsRUN/STOP. A tripped pump will not restart until the fault is cleared.

6 · Trend and alarm summary

  • Trend group: Heater group, Temperature cascade, Temperatures, BFW system, or Selected tag (PV, SP and OUT of the open faceplate). Window 5–60 min; each pen has its own range in the legend.
  • Alarm summary: newest unacknowledged first. Click a row to acknowledge it and open that instrument.

7 · Safety system (SIS)

Button / panelWhat it does
Reset SISClears a trip. Refused while the cause is still present.
Open XV-100Admits steam when every start permissive is green: SIS reset, BFW ≥ 50 m³/h, FIC-104 in MAN at ≤ 10 %, trap line open.
Close XV-100 (normal stop)Planned steam isolation, not counted as a trip.
Emergency shutdownImmediate trip: XV-100 closes, FIC-104 goes to MAN at 0 %, TIC-101 to MAN.
Trip conditionsAmber ● = present now; ▶ in red = first-out cause of the last trip.
Vent upgradesRev B: restriction orifice RO-101 gives a small continuous vent. Rev C: automatic air vent AAV-101 that opens when its line runs cool, plus TI-102 and alarm TAL-102.

8 · Field

  • Pumps P-101A/B. Hand valves: V-104 air vent at the top of the far end of the shell; V-103 trap bypass; V-105 shell drain to sewer; V-101 and V-102 trap block valves.
  • Walk along the shell: skin temperatures at the steam end, the top of the far end and the bottom.
  • Tap test: finds a liquid level under the insulation (result in 1 min). Bucket test: condensate rate leaving the trap set (result in 2 min).
  • Look at the trap and bypass, look at the vent, and local gauges (PG, TG) that are independent of the DCS transmitters.

9 · Exercises

  • Load an exercise: the plant is reset to its starting state; faults appear on their own schedule. Some troubleshooting cases start part-way through a problem that began before you arrived.
  • Procedure tracker: steps tick with their time when the simulator sees them done (! = done out of order). Tick Communicated and press Finish and grade (it also grades itself at the time limit).
  • What-if, Trend matching, Scrambles, DCS reading sheet: as labelled; each result goes to the Debrief tab.

10 · Debrief and data export

  • Debrief: score with each deduction, performance, exercise grades, fault recovery times and the event log (filter and copy).
  • Data export: tick the data sets, choose range and interval, then download. Files are UTF-8 CSV with three # header lines. Nothing is kept after you close the page.

Trainee workbook · BFW Steam Heater Ver 1

Work through Parts A to G in order. Record your answers and evidence (screenshots, CSV files) as you go; your report is built from them.

1 Purpose · 2 The unit · 3 Control scheme · 4 Safety systems · 5 Operating rules · 6 Activities A–G · 7 Grading · 8 Report checklist

1 · Purpose

This workbook trains you to operate, monitor and troubleshoot a steam-heated shell-and-tube heater (E-101) that preheats boiler feed water with low-pressure flash steam recovered from an upstream plant. By the end you should be able to:

  1. Read the P&ID and the DCS displays and state the normal value and alarm limits of every key tag.
  2. Explain how steam pressure, saturation temperature, UA and BFW load set the outlet temperature, and predict the direction every key variable moves after a disturbance.
  3. Start up the heater safely: air out of the shell, slow warm-up, cascade control in service.
  4. Recognise an abnormal situation from alarms, trends and field checks, keep the unit safe, and find the root cause with a systematic six-stage method.
  5. Propose a permanent improvement and support it with exported data.

2 · The unit

BFW from TK-101 is pumped by P-101A (P-101B spare) through FV-101A and flowmeter FT-101 into the tubes of E-101 (one pass, 100 tubes) and on to the boiler house. The recycle valve FV-101B opens as FV-101A closes so the pump is never dead-headed. Flash steam from the header passes the SIS shut-off valve XV-100, flowmeter FT-104 and control valve FV-104 into the shell, where it condenses on the tubes. Condensate leaves at the bottom through block valve V-101, strainer Y-101, trap ST-101 and V-102 to the condensate return header; V-103 bypasses the trap and V-105 drains the shell to sewer. Air vent V-104 sits on top of the shell at the end furthest from the steam inlet. VB-101 lets air in if the shell falls below atmospheric; PSV-100 protects the shell.

Values are the model's design point with noise off. The flow rates, header pressure and exchanger rating are engineering assumptions chosen to be consistent with a 100-tube single-pass heater, a 70 °C BFW target and a shell running near 105 kPa g; the shell runs at the saturation pressure needed for the duty, below the 200 kPa g header.

3 · Control scheme

LoopMeasuresMovesValve on air failureNotes
FIC-101BFW flow FT-101FV-101A (and FV-101B = 100 − OUT)Fail openKeeps water flowing through the tubes if the signal is lost.
TIC-101BFW outlet TT-101Remote set point of FIC-104—Primary of the cascade. Tracks FIC-104 when FIC-104 is not in CAS.
FIC-104Steam flow FT-104FV-104Fail closedSecondary of the cascade. The shell pressure floats to whatever condenses this steam.
V-104, V-103, V-105, V-101, V-102—Field hand valves—Vent, trap bypass, drain and trap isolation; operated from the Field tab.

Why the shell pressure matters. The shell sits at the saturation temperature of its pressure. With a clean exchanger it needs only ≈ 105 kPa g (121 °C) to make 70 °C. If part of the surface stops working, TIC-101 asks for more steam and the pressure rises toward the 200 kPa g header; once FV-104 is fully open there is no margin left and TT-101 falls.

4 · Safety systems

SIS: XV-100 opens only from IDLE with every start permissive met. Any trip closes XV-100, sets FIC-104 to MAN at 0 % and TIC-101 to MAN, and latches the first-out cause. Reset needs the cause to clear; steam is then readmitted slowly by hand.

Alarm limits

Water hammer happens when steam is admitted fast into a cold shell, or onto a shell flooded with condensate. It is logged, alarmed and costs 10 points each time.

5 · Operating rules

  1. Air out before heat in. Open V-104 before admitting steam and keep it open while you raise the steam, until dry steam blows.
  2. Warm up slowly. FIC-104 in MAN at 5–10 % for 2–3 minutes before raising the steam.
  3. Water first, steam second; steam off first, water off last. Never put steam on stagnant water.
  4. Watch the margin, not only the temperature. FV-104 creeping open and PI-100 rising while TT-101 is on set point means the exchanger is losing surface.
  5. Close the heat balance. Steam × latent heat should equal F·cp·ΔT of the water. If not, a meter is wrong or steam is escaping.
  6. Check two instruments before you believe one: TT-101 vs TIAH-108 and TG-101; TI-100 vs Tsat(PI-100); FIC-104 vs the bucket test.
  7. The shell has no level transmitter. Use the tap test, the trap bypass and the bottom skin temperature.
  8. Acknowledge every alarm and say out loud what it means.

6 · Activities

Part A · Familiarisation (about 20 min)

  1. Open the P&ID. Trace the BFW, steam, condensate and vent paths and list every instrument and valve on each.
  2. Visit the four DCS displays. Sketch the temperature profile along the tubes and write down the design NTU.
  3. Complete the DCS reading sheet (Exercises tab). Graded out of 15.
  4. Do a round on the Field tab: walk the shell, read the local gauges, look at the trap. Download a snapshot CSV.

Part B · What-if predictions (about 20 min)

For each event predict ↑ / ↓ / = for all eight variables before pressing Check my predictions. Explain every wrong prediction with a heat balance, the saturation curve or the valve and pump curves.

Part C · Cold startup (graded, limit 45 min simulated)

Load Cold startup through the SIS from Procedures. The tracker ticks steps as you complete them:

    Part D · Training exercises

    For each exercise record: first alarm and time, the first variable you noticed, what you did, and the recovery time in Debrief.

    Part E · Think EQUIPPED troubleshooting

    Each case gives only a situation. Work through the six stages and write your evidence for each:

    StageWhat you must produce
    1 EngageIs it dangerous or time-critical? Decide: keep running, safe-park or shut down, and say why.
    2 DefineProblem statement (what, where, when, how much, what did not change), IS / IS NOT table, and a measurable target.
    3 ExploreFundamentals: Tout = Ts − (Ts − Tin)·exp(−UA/F cp) — every cause must move Ts, UA, F cp, or the reading. Close the heat balance, compare instruments, list recent changes, read the trends and the clock of the problem.
    4 PlanAt least three working hypotheses written so they can fail, each with a test (tag, field check, what result kills it), ordered by safety, time and cost.
    5 Do itRun the tests, record results, name the root cause, apply the fix; predict the response before each move.
    6 Look backCompare prediction with result, and propose a change that stops it happening again (you may test rev B or rev C on the SIS tab).

    Part F · Trend matching and scrambles

    Match four unlabelled trend sets to their events and justify each from the six pens. Put the scramble steps in order.

    Part G · Data and report

    For your Part C run and one Part E case, download the run data (all data sets, 10 s) and the event log. Plot TT-101, FIC-104, FV-104 and PI-100 against time, and the NTU from temperatures before and after your fix.

    7 · How you are graded

    The continuous score starts at 100 and loses points while steam is on (during startup, shutdown and emergency procedures the temperature and steam-loss deductions are paused):

    DeductionRate
    BFW outlet more than 1 °C from its targetup to 3 points/min, growing with the error
    Steam wasted at vent, trap, bypass or drain above 5 % of the steam0.5 points/min
    BFW outlet above 90 °C5 points/min
    Alarm left unacknowledged over 60 s0.3 points/min per alarm
    Unplanned SIS trip caused by operation (trips that follow an equipment failure are not charged)15 points each
    Water hammer10 points each

    Procedures, the reading sheet, what-if, trend matching and scrambles are graded separately under Exercise grades in the Debrief tab.

    8 · Report checklist

    • Part A sketches, reading-sheet score and snapshot CSV.
    • Part B predictions with corrections.
    • Part C procedure grade, time to line out, and trend plots.
    • Part D table for every exercise.
    • Part E six-stage worksheet for each assigned case, with evidence (trends, heat balance, field checks).
    • Debrief screenshot: score, deductions and exercise grades.
    • One recommended improvement, with before/after data.

          1 What a BFD is · 2 The diagram · 3 The blocks · 4 Streams · 5 Balances on the boundary · 6 From BFD to PFD

          1 · What a block flow diagram is

          A block flow diagram (BFD) is the simplest drawing of a process: each operation is a box, each main stream is a line with an arrow, and the streams carry numbers that point to a table. It answers what goes where and how much, before anyone decides what the equipment looks like. The engineering drawings of a unit are read in this order:

          DrawingWhat it showsWhat it leaves outUsed forOn this simulator
          BFDOperations as blocks, main streams, stream numbers, overall flowsEquipment shapes, valves, instrumentsConcept, overall mass and energy balance, explaining the unitThis tab; section 2 of the Process tab
          PFDEvery major equipment item with its symbol and tag, control valves, stream flags (flow, T, P), a heat and material balanceHand valves, drains, most instruments, line sizesProcess design, sizing, HAZIDPFD tab (BFW-PFD-100)
          P&IDEvery pipe, valve, instrument loop, fail position, trip and relief deviceFlows and conditions (in the data sheets instead)Detailed design, HAZOP, construction, operationP&ID tab; the live copy is the DCS console

          2 · The block flow diagram

          Streams 1–8 are numbered as in the stream table below and on the PFD (stream 8, the losses, is closed at design). Solid lines carry process fluid or steam; dashed lines are utilities or paths that are closed at design.

          3 · The blocks

          BlockOperationInOutWhat it does in this unit

          4 · Streams: Design and Now

          Design comes from the model at the design point (noise off); Now is the live plant. The numbers move as you operate the unit or when a fault is present.

          #StreamPhasekg/hT °CP kPa g
          DesignNowDesignNowDesignNow

          5 · Balances on the block boundary

          Draw one envelope around the whole diagram. Two fluids cross it and never mix: water (streams 3 → 4) and steam (streams 6 → 7 and 8). So the unit has two separate mass balances and one energy balance that links them: the latent heat given up by the steam is the sensible heat taken by the water.

          Overall mass balance, kg/h

          6 · From BFD to PFD

          • Each block becomes one or more equipment items with a tag and a symbol: the block "E-101" becomes a shell-and-tube exchanger with the steam in the shell; "Y-101 · ST-101" becomes a strainer and a trap.
          • The control valves appear on the lines they throttle (FV-101A, FV-101B, FV-104) with the shut-off valve XV-100.
          • Each numbered stream gets a flag with flow, temperature and pressure at design, so the drawing carries its own heat and material balance.
          • The P&ID then adds every hand valve, drain, vent, instrument loop, trip and relief device. See the PFD and P&ID tabs.

          Process flow diagram (PFD) · BFW-PFD-100

          1 What a PFD adds · 2 The drawing · 3 Equipment list · 4 Stream flags and the model · 5 Reading the PFD · 6 From PFD to P&ID

          1 · What a PFD adds to the block flow diagram

          • Equipment symbols and tags (ISO 10628 conventions): the exchanger is drawn as a shell-and-tube with the steam on the shell side, the pumps as a pair, the trap and strainer as small items on the condensate line.
          • Control and shut-off valves on the lines they act on, with fail positions where they matter (FV-101A fails open, FV-104 fails closed).
          • Stream flags: flow, temperature and pressure at the design point on every numbered stream. The drawing carries its own heat and material balance.
          • Battery limits: where each stream comes from and goes to outside the unit (flash-steam header, boiler house, condensate return, vent and relief to a safe location).

          A PFD leaves out hand valves, drains, instrument loops, line sizes and most instruments; those belong on the P&ID.

          2 · The drawing

          PDF (A4) PowerPoint (editable) SVG PNG Files in the same folder as this page (offline or GitHub Pages).

            3 · Equipment list

            TagEquipmentSymbolRole in this unit

            4 · Stream flags and the model

            The flags on the drawing are the model's design point, rounded. The Now columns come from the live plant: when you change a set point or a fault develops, the drawing stays at design and the plant moves away from it.

            #Stream1000 kg/hT °CP kPa g
            FlagNowFlagNowFlagNow

            5 · Reading the PFD

            • Two fluids, never mixed. Follow the water 1 → 3 → 4 along the bottom and the steam 5 → 6 → 7 across the top and down through the shell. They meet only through the tube walls.
            • Flow in = flow out on each side. Stream 3 equals stream 4 and stream 6 equals stream 7 at design: nothing is lost through the vent, bypass or drain (stream 8 carries no flag).
            • Pressure falls along each path. Water: pump discharge → FV-101A → tubes → boiler house. Steam: header → FV-104 → shell → trap → return header. The shell pressure between FV-104 and the trap is not set by any controller: it floats.
            • The recycle is not a loss. Stream 2 returns to TK-101, so the pumps move stream 1 = streams 2 + 3.

            Fail positions and sparesFV-101A FO, FV-104 FC, P-101B spare

            1 · Operability and the operating window

            Process operability means the plant has the capacity and flexibility to reach a range of operating conditions safely, reliably, profitably, with good dynamic performance and product quality. The operating window is the range of achievable steady-state operation: every set point is held and no limit is crossed. Four things shape it.

            The variables of E-101

            ClassVariable (tag)DesignWhy it is in this class

            2 · Variability: the design basis the window must cover

            "The abnormal is normal." A window is only as good as the list of changes it was sized for. The five sources of variability, written as a design-basis memorandum for E-101 (ranges come from the page's alarms and fault library; frequencies are teaching values):

            SourceWhat changes on E-101Range used hereHow oftenCovered by

            A single human error must not cause an unsafe condition and must not stay undetected. That is why the bounds in part 3 carry alarms and, where the damage is fast (overheated BFW to the boiler house, shell overpressure, steam on stagnant water), trips on XV-100.

            3 · Bounds and the integrity operating window

            The bounds are the frame of the window. A hard bound cannot be crossed without damage or a trip (shell overpressure, vacuum, overheated BFW, steam on stagnant water). A soft bound can be crossed for a while, but something degrades (flooded tubes and water hammer, gas-blanketed tubes, wasted steam). A capacity bound is the end of a handle's travel. The table shows the limit, the design value, the live value and the margin now as a fraction of the margin at design.

            BoundKindWhy it existsLimitDesignNowMargin now ÷ margin at design

            Reading the IOW. Inside the target range the heater holds 70 °C with room on every handle. Between the target and the standard limit it is still safe, but time counts (flooded tubes invite water hammer, a valve near its stop cannot answer the next disturbance). Past the critical limit failure is quick; that is where the trips on XV-100 act (Safety layers tab).

            4 · Design for the worst case, and a live point check

            Equipment is sized for the worst case of the variability it must handle. For a heat exchanger (Q = U A ΔT) the worst case for the heating medium is the highest flow at the coldest inlet with the most fouling; for the condensate side it is the lowest load, when the shell pressure falls and the trap has the least pressure to push with. Pick a case, or set your own point: the page runs a copy of this model to steady state (cascade TIC-101 → FIC-104 in AUTO at 70 °C, trips switched off so limits can be seen, the change ramped in over 15 min) and checks every bound.

            5 · Capacity and turndown

            A small heater that only just meets the design point is cheap but has no window; a large one has a window but costs capital, and a steam heater that is too large runs at a low shell pressure. The capacity must be safe, protect the equipment and meet quality for the base case and frequently occurring variability; lower production is acceptable in rare cases; stop for extreme ones. Turndown ratio = normal maximum ÷ normal minimum, where "normal" means sustainable without hazard or damage.

            Each element has its own BFW-flow range. The heater's range is the overlap, so it is always narrower than any single element's. Ranges below come from a sweep of 2.5 m³/h steps at the design BFW inlet and header, interpolated between runs.

            ElementTurndown or rangeability on E-101TypicalFlexibility class

            7 · Type II and Type III: the disturbances E-101 can absorb

            Now the controlled variables sit at their set points (FIC-101 on the BFW demand, TIC-101 at 70 °C through FIC-104) while the disturbances move. Type II reads the handle positions each disturbance needs; Type III keeps only the points where every handle is inside its range and every bound holds, and colours the rest by the bound that fails first (root cause before symptom).

            8 · Monte Carlo operating window

            The recipe: (1) simulate the base case, (2) replace the uncertain inputs by samples from their distributions and repeat, (3) mark each sample inside or outside against every bound, (4) report the fraction and show it. Here each sample is interpolated in the Type II grids of part 7 (BFW flow × inlet temperature × header pressure, for the gas case chosen in part 7), and every bound is checked on the interpolated steady state.

            9 · Manipulated variables: enough, strong, independent, fast

            With n adjustable handles and m variables to hold: n = m gives a finite window with each point exactly specified; n < m gives no window (at best the design point) and is not an acceptable design; n > m leaves extra freedom that can be used to optimise.

Gains, capacities and responses come from runs on copies of this simulator's model; the curves in parts 4 and 5 are drawn from the model's own equations (pump, FV-101A/B, FV-104, heat transfer).               1 What flexibility is · 2 How many · 3 Where · 4 Fluid flow · 5 Heat transfer · 6 Production rate · 7 Control strategies · 8 How much · 9 Recommendations

              1 · What flexibility is

              Flexibility is the ability of a plant to operate reliably across a wide range of rates and conditions without losing quantity or quality. Some controlled variables are held at their set points while disturbances arrive; flexibility is what lets us steer the process after the equipment has been built.

              Without flexibility the heater does not respond to set-point changes and passes every disturbance (a colder inlet, a weaker header, a new boiler demand) on to the feed-water temperature. With flexibility it reaches its set points and compensates the disturbances.

              How it is provided

              • Spare capacity in pumps, valves, exchanger area, trap capacity.
              • Adjustable utility flows: here the flash steam (and, on the other side, the vent to atmosphere).
              • By-passes and recycles that send part of a flow around equipment: FV-101B recycle, V-103 trap bypass.

              Four design questions: how many handles, where, which tools (valves, speed, level, by-pass), and how much capacity.

              The flexibility register of E-101

              HandleWhat it adjustsKind of flexibilityAt designSpare at designStatus

              2 · How many handles? Degrees of freedom

              A successful design needs number of adjustable handles ≥ number of variables to be held. The maximum number of controlled variables equals the degrees of freedom; the minimum number of handles equals the number of variables we insist on.

              Each held variable needs a handle with an independent causal path to it. Interaction is allowed as long as every desired point can still be reached. Three cases:

              4 · Flexibility for fluid flow

              For liquids the flow settles where the pump's pressure rise equals the losses: F = √(ΔP / ((fL/D + Kvalve + ΣKj) ρ/2g)). Only the valve term (or the pump speed) is adjustable. On E-101 the BFW side is a liquid system with a complementary recycle; the steam side is a gas valve feeding a floating shell.

              4a · BFW: FV-101A with the FV-101B recycle, or pump speed

              4b · Steam: FV-104 installed characteristic (the model's own equation)

              5 · Flexibility for heat transfer

              Q = U A ΔT: flexibility can act on U (a flow changes a film coefficient), on A (area in service: a condensate level covers tubes, a gas pocket blankets them) or on ΔT (the steam's saturation temperature, a by-pass that mixes).

              Term in E-101What sets itHandle todayAlternative handle

              Three ways to hold 70 °C, and what each costs

              WayHow the duty is trimmedOn E-101
              a · Steam pressure (shell floats)FV-104 throttles the steam; the shell pressure and its saturation temperature fall until ε F cp (Ts − Tin) equals the dutyAs built. Fast, simple, dry shell; but at low load the shell falls toward the return header and the trap stops draining.
              b · Condensate flooding (area)The steam valve stays open, the shell sits near the header; a valve on the condensate raises the level and covers tubesAlternative. Drainage is never lost and the condensate leaves subcooled; but the level responds slowly and a flooded shell is where water hammer starts.
              c · BFW by-pass (mixing)The shell sits near the header; part of the BFW goes round E-101 and mixes with the hotter heated streamAlternative. Fast (mixing) and the shell stays high; but the tubes run hotter than 70 °C and the three-way valve is new equipment.

              6 · Flexibility for production rate

              At steady state material must balance in every unit and in the whole plant. One flexible variable sets the rate; every other flow follows automatically, and measured flows are never simply matched to each other (meter errors would accumulate). Level and pressure show inventory.

              Guiding principleE-101

              HAZID · Hazard Identification of the BFW heater

              Teaching slide deck · what HAZID is, the PFD and its seven study areas, the guideword checklist, bow-tie prevention and mitigation, the major accident hazards of a steam heater and the studies that follow.
              Open the deck ↗Same folder (offline / GitHub Pages)
              1 What HAZID is · 2 Method · 3 PFD and study areas · 4 Guideword checklist · 5 Hazard register · 6 Major accident hazards · 7 From HAZID to HAZOP

              A plant-level, checklist-driven identification of the major hazards around E-101, done before (and wider than) the detailed HAZOP. It uses the same example risk matrix as the HAZOP tab; a real study uses the owner's matrix and a multidisciplinary team.

              1 · What HAZID is and where it sits

              HAZID (Hazard Identification) is a structured brainstorm of what could go badly wrong across the whole facility, including its surroundings, people and environment. It is done early (concept and front-end design) on the PFD, the plot plan and the design basis, so that the major hazards shape the design before the details are fixed. It asks broad questions ("what hazards exist in the steam and condensate area?"), where HAZOP asks detailed ones ("what if the condensate level is higher than intended?").

              A steam heater holds no flammable inventory, so its major hazards are different from those of a fired heater: stored energy (steam and hot water that flash when released), pressure from two sides (the steam header on the shell, the BFW pumps on the tubes), water hammer, vacuum when the steam is cut, and the knock-on effect on the boiler house that depends on the BFW.

              HAZIDHAZOP
              WhenConcept / FEED, and before major changesDetailed design, P&ID frozen; revalidation
              DrawingPFD, plot planP&ID, cause-and-effect chart
              BreakdownAreas / systemsNodes with one design intent
              PromptGuideword checklist by hazard category (natural, external, process, utilities, health, occupational, environment, operations)Guide word × parameter (NO flow, MORE pressure, …)
              ScopeProcess and non-process hazards, site and surroundingsProcess deviations and operability
              OutputHazard register, list of major accident hazards, studies to do next (HAZOP, relief review, SIL, layout)Worksheets and recommendations per deviation
              ReferenceISO 17776 (major accident hazard management in design; HAZID and its checklist); company HSE practiceIEC 61882

              2 · Method

              1. Define scope and basis: E-101 with TK-101, P-101A/B and the recycle, the steam branch from the flash-steam header, the shell with vent, vacuum breaker and relief, the condensate trap set to the return header, the SIS, the utilities and the site; the example risk matrix.
              2. Divide the plant into areas on the PFD (section 3).
              3. Apply the guideword checklist to each area (section 4): for every category ask whether the hazard exists here, what could release it (cause / threat) and what would follow (top event and outcome).
              4. Record existing controls, split into prevention (stops the top event) and mitigation (limits the outcome), as in a bow-tie.
              5. Rank the risk (S × L with the controls) and flag major accident hazards (MAH): events that could cause multiple fatalities or major damage, or that escalate beyond the unit (here: into the boiler house).
              6. Assign actions and further studies: design changes, HAZOP nodes, relief and vacuum review, SIL assessment, maintenance procedures.

                  1 Control objectives · 2 The feedback loop · 3 Variables of E-101 · 4 Degrees of freedom · 5 Loops on the P&ID · 6 How the loops were chosen · 7 Loop structures · 8 P, PI and PID · 9 Tuning lab

                  1 · Control objectives (ต้องการควบคุมอะไร และเพราะอะไร)

                  Control design starts from objectives, not from instruments. They are ranked: a lower objective is never met by giving up a higher one. On E-101 the first two ranks are held by the SIS and by the way the unit is operated; the loops look after ranks 3 to 5.

                  2 · The feedback loop: parts and vocabulary

                  In this simulator OUT is always shown as % open. FV-101A fails open, so the signal to its actuator is inverted in the field; the operator never sees that inversion. The fail position is chosen for the safe state and is independent of the controller action: both FV-101A (fail open) and FV-104 (fail closed) sit in reverse-acting loops.

                  3 · Variables of E-101 classified

                  Every variable is one of: a controlled variable (CV) held at a set point, a manipulated variable (MV) moved by a controller or by the operator, a disturbance (DV) set by the surroundings, a variable that is only indicated or alarmed, or an independent trip measurement read by the SIS.

                  4 · Degrees of freedom (DOF)

                  Why it matters. The degrees of freedom tell the designer how many variables can be held independently. Try to control more CVs than there are independent MVs and controllers fight over one valve; control fewer and some variable drifts wherever the disturbances push it.

                  NDOF = Nvariables − Nindependent equations    and    NDOF = Ndisturbances (fixed by the surroundings) + Nmanipulated

                  For control the useful count is the control DOF = the number of independent manipulated variables, which for a process unit is the number of independent valves (and speeds, dampers) that can be set continuously.

                  4.1 DOF of E-101 at steady state

                  4.2 Check on the model

                  Each handle is moved on its own on a copy of the model at design (all controllers in MAN), and the new steady state is compared with design. Five independent columns of effect mean five independent handles.

                  Computing on a copy of the model…

                  4.3 How each DOF is used

                  4.4 DOF of each loop

                  • A feedback loop uses one DOF: it turns "valve position is free" into "CV = SP". The SP becomes the new free input, given by the operator, the boiler house or a higher controller.
                  • Cascade does not create a DOF. TIC-101 → FIC-104 → FV-104 is still the one valve FV-104: the inner loop fixes the steam flow, the outer loop chooses which steam flow. Feedforward and ratio act through the same valve too.
                  • FV-101B is not an extra DOF. It has no signal of its own: it moves as 100 − OUT of FIC-101, so the pair is one handle.
                  • The shell pressure is not a DOF. Nothing sets it; it floats to the saturation pressure at which the tubes condense the steam that comes in (section 4.2 shows it returning to the same value from any start).
                  • A controller in MAN gives its DOF back to the operator (loop open). A valve at 0 % or 100 % (saturated) loses its DOF: the CV is then uncontrolled. Two controllers must never move one valve at the same time unless a selector or split range decides which one acts.

                    8 · Control modes: P, PI and PID (แนวทางการควบคุม P, PI, PID)

                    The simulator's controller (pid() in the model) uses the ideal PID form with every signal in % of the instrument span:

                    OUT(t) = Kc [ e(t) + (1/Ti) ∫e dt − Td dPV/dt ] + bias,   e = SP − PV (reverse action)

                    • % of span: PV and SP are converted to % of the range (FIC-101 , TIC-101 , FIC-104 ), so Kc is in % OUT per % PV and does not depend on engineering units.
                    • Derivative on PV, not on error, so a set-point change gives no derivative kick; the derivative term is filtered with a time constant Td/8.
                    • Anti-windup: when OUT is clamped at 0 or 100 %, the integral is reset so that OUT sits exactly on the limit; it starts moving back as soon as the error changes sign.
                    • Bumpless transfer: on any mode change the integral is initialised so OUT does not jump. When FIC-104 is not in CAS, TIC-101 tracks: its OUT follows the FIC-104 set point, ready for a bumpless return to cascade.
                    • Ti = 0 switches the integral off (P only); the bias then keeps the OUT it had, which is why P-only control leaves an offset after a load change.

                    8.1 What each term does

                    ModeActionGoodBadTypical use
                    P (proportional)OUT change ∝ error now.Simple, immediate, stable at low gain.Offset: after a load change the error settles at e = Δload / (1 + KcK), not zero. High gain → oscillation.Averaging level control, where offset does not matter. (ST-101 behaves like a P-only level controller.)
                    PI (+ integral)Adds the accumulated error; keeps moving OUT until the error is zero.No offset. The industrial default.Slower, more overshoot if Ti is short; windup when the valve saturates (needs anti-windup).All three E-101 loops.
                    PID (+ derivative)Adds action ∝ rate of change of PV; anticipates.Faster, less overshoot on slow, lag-dominated loops with a clean signal.Amplifies noise; derivative on error kicks on SP changes (hence derivative on PV).Slow temperature loops; rarely on flow.

                    8.3 Tuning from a step test (FOPDT model)

                    Put the loop in MAN, step OUT, record PV. Fit a first-order-plus-dead-time model G(s) = K e−θs/(τs + 1): K = ΔPV/ΔOUT (both in % of span); from the times to 28.3 % and 63.2 % of the final change, τ = 1.5 (t63 − t28), θ = t63 − τ. Then the lambda (IMC) PI rule with a chosen closed-loop time constant λ:

                    Kc = τ / [K(λ + θ)],   Ti = τ    (λ = τ for a smooth loop, λ = τ/3 for a tight one)

                    Presets

                    Things to try

                    1. Offset. TIC-101, load "BFW flow 100 → 110 m³/h": click Simulator tuning, then P only. TT-101 settles about 2.6 °C below 70 °C and stays there; with the simulator's PI it dips 2.1 °C and is back on set point within about 4 minutes. The integral term removes the offset. P only on the set-point step 70 → 72 °C stops about 1.2 °C short, as e = ΔSP / (1 + KcK) = 2 / (1 + 1.2 × 0.59) predicts.
                    2. What the inner loop does. TIC-101, load "steam header 200 → 160 kPa g", P only: no offset this time. The header disturbance enters the inner loop, and FIC-104 (a PI) removes it before TT-101 needs to move.
                    3. Inner loop speed. Same header test with the simulator's tuning: TT-101 dips about 1.7 °C. Set the inner loop to Kc 1, Ti 2 s: the dip falls to about 0.6 °C. A cascade works best when the inner loop is several times faster than the outer one (section 8.4 shows how slow the as-built FIC-104 is).
                    4. Reset time. TIC-101 set-point step, Ti 45 → 30 → 15 s: overshoot about 0.16 → 0.36 → 0.81 °C. The lambda and tight presets give no overshoot. Tuning is a trade-off, not a single right answer.
                    5. Derivative. TIC-101 set-point step, PID with Td 10 s: almost no change, because the dead time is small compared with the time constant.
                    6. Feedforward. TIC-101, load "BFW flow 100 → 110 m³/h", structure cascade + feedforward: the dip halves (about 2.1 → 1.0 °C), and for the inlet −7 °C load about 2.6 → 1.3 °C. The feedback loop still removes what the feedforward calculation gets wrong.
                    7. A slow flow loop. FIC-104, set-point step +500 kg/h: with the simulator's tuning the flow is still about 20 kg/h short after 5 minutes; Kc 1, Ti 2 s settles in about 30 s. The lambda preset is faster still but overshoots about 60 kg/h (12 % of the step).
                    8. Too much gain on a flow loop. FIC-101, set-point step 100 → 110 m³/h with Kc 2, Ti 1 s: the flow overshoots by about 3.3 m³/h (a third of the step) and the valve swings widely.

                    HAZOP · Hazard and Operability Study of E-101

                    Teaching slide deck · IEC 61882 phases, the six nodes of the BFW heater, guide words, a worked worksheet row, safeguards, the dynamic checks on the simulator and the follow-up to LOPA.
                    Open the deck ↗Same folder (offline / GitHub Pages)
                    1 Standard and method · 2 Team and documents · 3 Nodes · 4 Guide words and parameters · 5 Risk matrix · 6 Worksheets · 7 Coverage check · 8 Recommendations · 9 Dynamic check on the simulator · 10 Follow-up and close-out

                    A teaching HAZOP of the flash-steam BFW heater as drawn on the P&ID tab, done node by node with the IEC 61882 guide words. Risk ranking uses the example matrix in section 5 (the same one as the HAZID tab); a real study uses the owner's corporate matrix, a multidisciplinary team and the as-built documents.

                    1 · Standard and method (IEC 61882)

                    HAZOP is a structured, team-based examination of a defined system. Each part of the design is compared with its design intent; guide words combined with process parameters generate deviations; for each meaningful deviation the team records causes, consequences, existing safeguards and, where the risk is not acceptable, recommendations. It finds hazards (harm to people, environment, assets) and operability problems (the heater cannot deliver hot BFW, or cannot be run as intended).

                    ReferenceWhat it contributes
                    IEC 61882:2016 Hazard and operability studies (HAZOP studies) – Application guideDefinitions, the four phases (definition, preparation, examination, documentation and follow-up), guide words, team roles, recording
                    CCPS Guidelines for Hazard Evaluation ProceduresWorksheet format, node selection, consequences judged without safeguards, risk ranking, link to LOPA
                    IEC 61511 (functional safety, SIS)How HAZOP scenarios feed LOPA and SIL targets for the XV-100 trips FSLL-101, TSHH-108 and PSHH-100
                    ISO 31000 / owner's risk matrixRisk criteria used to decide whether safeguards are adequate
                    TEMA / ASME Section VIII, API 520/521Shell-and-tube exchanger design pressures, the tube-rupture ("two-thirds") rule, relief sizing for PSV-100 and vacuum design of the shell
                    Thailand: Department of Industrial Works regulation on hazard identification, risk assessment and risk-management plans (B.E. 2543)Legal requirement to identify hazards (HAZOP is an accepted method) and to prepare risk-management plans for factories
                    OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119 (PSM), where applicableProcess hazard analysis revalidated at least every five years (a steam heater is usually covered only as part of a larger process)

                    The four phases

                    1. Definition: scope E-101 with TK-101, P-101A/B, FIC-101 and the recycle, the steam branch from the flash-steam header (PI-105) through XV-100 and FV-104, the shell with its vent, vacuum breaker and relief, and the condensate trap set to the return header; the SIS (XV-100 trips). Excluded: the upstream flash-steam plant, the condensate return system beyond the header and the boiler house (their interfaces are recorded as causes and consequences). Objectives, team, risk matrix.
                    2. Preparation: collect the P&ID, PFD, heat and material balance, trip (cause-and-effect) list, alarm list, procedures and datasheets; divide the unit into nodes; write each node's design intent; choose parameters and guide words.
                    3. Examination: node → design intent → parameter → guide word → is the deviation meaningful? → causes → consequences assuming the safeguards fail → existing safeguards → rank the risk → recommend → next guide word. Every meaningful deviation is recorded, including those with adequate safeguards (full recording), so the reasoning can be audited.
                    4. Documentation and follow-up: worksheets, recommendation register with owners and dates, close-out, revalidation after changes (MOC) or periodically.

                    Consequences are written with no credit for safeguards (worst credible case); the likelihood L is then judged with the listed safeguards working as designed.

                    2 · Team and documents

                    RoleResponsibility
                    HAZOP leader (chair)Independent of the design; runs the method, keeps the team on the node, decides when a deviation is covered

                    Documents for this study: P&ID tab (rev A, with the rev B / rev C vent upgrades), Process tab (stream table and duty), HAZID tab (PFD BFW-PFD-100 and the major hazards), Design and Control loop design tabs (when present), Workbook tab (alarm list and trip settings), and the start-up, shutdown and emergency-shutdown procedures in the Exercises tab.

                    3 · Nodes

                    A node is a section of the plant with one design intent. Boundaries are put where the intent changes: the pumps raise pressure, FV-101A sets the BFW rate, the tubes heat the water, FV-104 throttles the steam, the shell condenses it, the trap holds steam in and lets condensate out. The procedures get their own node, because start-up, shutdown and restart create deviations that steady operation does not.

EARLY / LATE / BEFORE / AFTER apply mainly to the procedure node N6. The right-hand columns confirm that flow, pressure and temperature (or their equivalents) were examined in every process node.

                    8 · Recommendation register

                    9 · Dynamic check of selected deviations on the simulator

                    A conventional HAZOP judges consequences qualitatively. Here selected deviations are run on copies of the E-101 model from the design point with the existing safeguards active (alarms, SIS trips, controllers in their normal modes, no operator action) for up to 30 min, or 30 s past a trip. Alarms are evaluated from the page's alarm list every second, with the same suppression as the console (steam alarms only while steaming, BFW alarms only with a pump running). The runs show whether the safeguards act before harm, and how much time the operator has.

                    Runs when this tab is opened.

                    What the runs tell the HAZOP team

                    • Waiting for the runs…

                    10 · Follow-up and close-out

                    • Each recommendation gets an owner and a due date; the owner answers accepted and done, accepted with an alternative (with justification) or rejected (with justification agreed by the HAZOP leader and the plant manager).
                    • High scenarios whose protection relies on instrumented trips or on PSV-100 (shell overpressure from the steam side, tube rupture, loss of BFW to the boiler house, water hammer) go to LOPA to set the required SIL of the XV-100 trips (IEC 61511) and to confirm the relief case.
                    • Any change (putting rev B RO-101 or rev C AAV-101 in service, a shell level transmitter, a new trip or a changed set point) goes through management of change, which checks whether the HAZOP must be updated.
                    • Interfaces: the loss-of-BFW and hot-BFW consequences are passed to the boiler-house HAZOP; header-pressure causes to the upstream flash-steam plant; trap and return-header causes to the condensate-system owner.
                    • Revalidate periodically (typically every five years) and after incidents.
                    • Use the simulator to train operators on the scenarios the HAZOP found, and to check that the procedures and alarm responses really work (section 9).

                    Safety layers · layers of protection for E-101

                    Teaching slide deck · the six protection layers of the BFW heater, the layered P&ID, the trip matrix, the integrity operating window and relief rules.
                    Open the deck ↗Same folder (offline / GitHub Pages)
                    1 The six layers · 2 P&ID layer by layer · 3 What each layer does · 4 Integrity operating window · 5 Independence check · 6 Good practices · 7 Standards

                    Safety must cover failures of equipment (including the control system) and of people, and more than one failure at a time. The response should be limited, keeping production where possible. So protection is built in layers, each independent of the others, with more strength held in reserve as the event gets more serious. The layers here are applied to E-101, a shell-and-tube heater in which low-pressure flash steam condenses on the shell side and boiler feed water (BFW) is heated in the tubes. Set points and trip limits are read from the simulator model; values marked "assumed" are for teaching.

                    1 · The six layers

                    LayerJobAutomatic?Needs power / computer?Needs a person?
                    1 BPCSClosed-loop control keeps the process in its operating regionYesYesSupervises
                    2 AlarmsBring an unusual situation to the attention of a personNo actionYesYes: decides
                    3 SISStop part of the process (steam off)YesYes, but de-energise to tripNo (reset only)
                    4 ReliefPrevent excessive pressure or vacuum; divert material safelyYes, self-actuatingNoNo
                    5 ContainmentKeep released steam and hot water away from workers, community and environmentPassiveNoPartly
                    6 Emergency responseEvacuation, first aid for burns, general site fire fightingNoPartlyYes

                    Layers 1–4 are the independent protection layers of the automation and the pressure system. Layers 1–3 all need electrical power, computing and communication, so a power or computer failure could take out all three at once. That is why XV-100 closes when its solenoid loses power, why FV-104 fails closed on loss of instrument air, and why FV-101A fails open (water keeps flowing through the tubes). Relief, containment and emergency response are kept in reserve. Click a ring to open that layer on the P&ID.

                    5 · Independence check

                    Each layer must not share its sensor, logic or final element with the layer below; otherwise one failure can defeat both. An alarm that belongs to an SIS function may share the SIS sensor, because it sits on the SIS system; a trip that shares the control transmitter is a gap. The table was checked against the trip logic of the simulator (tripConditions()), not only against the drawing.

                    LOPA · reliability for safety, layers of protection analysis and bow-tie for E-101

                    Teaching slide deck · failure rate and PFD, reliability block diagrams of the E-101 trips, the LOPA equation worked on five BFW-heater scenarios, and the bow-tie as many LOPAs at once.
                    Open the deck ↗Same folder (offline / GitHub Pages)

                    The HAZOP tab says what can go wrong; this tab asks how often, and whether the safeguards are reliable enough. Failure data are the course's generic values; SIS trips use SIS-grade (dangerous undetected) rates. Every frequency that is not from the course table is marked "assumed" and is for teaching, not for design. Times and temperatures quoted from "the model" come from runs of the simulator itself.

                    Part A · Reliability for safety

                    A1 · Definitions

                    TermMeaningOn E-101
                    HazardInherent physical or chemical characteristic that can harm people, environment or property (CCPS)Steam and hot water under pressure; the BFW pump's shut-off head behind the tubes; a cold shell that steam can collapse or hammer
                    Hazardous eventRelease of material or energy that can cause harmShell rupture; tube rupture into the shell; steam hammer; BFW flashing at the deaerator
                    RiskRisk = consequence × frequencyA fatality (severity 5) that is tolerable only below 10−4 /yr
                    Tolerable / residual riskRisk accepted in context / risk left after protectionThe LOPA target frequency / the mitigated frequency
                    Reliability R(t)Probability of success during an interval of timeFSLL-101 working through a one-year test interval
                    PFDProbability of failure on demand; F(t) = 1 − R(t)The chance that XV-100 does not close when the BFW flow is lost
                    Deterministic / probabilistic analysisCan the design keep events within limits / what is the numerical risk and is it tolerablePSV-100 sized for the worst relief case / LOPA below

                    Is 99.9 % reliability good enough? For a 1-in-1000 failure it would mean an unsafe landing every day at a big airport. Safety needs both plant reliability (business continuity) and safety reliability (hazard prevention and mitigation).

                    A2 · Failure rate from a population

                    λ = ΔNf / (Ns · Δt): failures in the interval divided by the survivors and the interval length. 100 identical units (think of 100 steam traps) are drawn from a Weibull life model, R(t) = e−(t/α)β; β < 1 is burn-in, β = 1 the useful life (constant λ = 1/α, the exponential model), β > 1 wear-out.



                    A3 · R(t), PFD and proof testing

                    With a constant failure rate R(t) = e−λt and PFD(t) = F(t) = 1 − e−λt ≈ λt when PFD ≪ 0.1. A standby safeguard fails unseen, so its PFD grows until the next proof test restores it: PFDavg = (1/T)∫0Tλt dt = λT/2. MTTF = ∫R dt = 1/λ.


                    SIL (IEC 61511, demand mode)PFDavgRRF
                    SIL 110−2 – 10−110 – 100
                    SIL 210−3 – 10−2100 – 1 000
                    SIL 310−4 – 10−31 000 – 10 000

                    A4 · Reliability block diagrams

                    ConfigurationPFDReliabilityFailure rate / MTTFPFDavg over test interval T
                    Series (multi-component): any failure fails the pathPFDA + PFDBR1·R2λ = λ1 + λ2; MTTF = 1/(λ1+λ2)λT/2 (1oo1); λT (2oo2)
                    Parallel (redundancy): all paths must failPFDA × PFDBR1+R2−R1R2MTTF = 1/λ1+1/λ2−1/(λ1+λ2)(λT)²/3 (1oo2)
                    2-out-of-3 (complex system)PFDAPFDB+PFDBPFDC+PFDCPFDA——(λT)²

                    SIF calculator. A safety instrumented function is sensor → logic solver → final element in series; each subsystem can be redundant. All three E-101 trips share the logic solver I-100 and the single steam shut-off valve XV-100. Pick a trip, change the voting, the SIS-grade failure rates or the test interval. Improving reliability: diversity (different technologies), separation (no single point of failure), fail-safe design.

                    SubsystemVotingλ per channel (/yr)PFDavgShare

                    The course method for parallel systems. Three layers against the same hazard, each with an equivalent failure rate (sum of its blocks), combined as parallel systems through MTTF (inclusion–exclusion): 1/λsys = Σ1/λi − Σ1/(λi+λj) + 1/(λ1+λ2+λ3).

                    E-101 low BFW flow: BPCS = flow sensor 1.14 + controller 0.2 + control valve 0.6; alarm = flow sensor 1.14 + controller 0.2 + operator 1.0; SIS = SIS flow sensor 0.010 + SIS controller 0.001 + shutdown valve 0.020 + solenoid 0.004. The result is set by the most reliable branch. LOPA (Part B) treats the same layers differently: it multiplies the demand rate by each layer's PFD, and it gives no credit to a layer that shares its sensor with the initiating event — and on E-101 all three branches read the same FT-101.

                    A5 · Failure data used in this tab

                    EquipmentFailure mode / contextGeneric rate (/yr)SIS / safety-grade rate (/yr)

                    Sources used by the course: OREDA and the CCPS Guidelines for Initiating Events and Independent Protection Layers. A generic rate counts all failure modes; an SIS rate counts only dangerous undetected failures of certified equipment. Millions of unit-hours are needed for a confident rate. A generic all-modes rate put into λT/2 is not a PFD: an alarm on a 1.14 /yr flow sensor would come out above 0.5, which is why alarm and BPCS layers take the fixed CCPS credit of 0.1 instead.

                    Part B · Layers of protection analysis (LOPA)

                    B1 · The method

                    1. Take a scenario from the HAZOP (cause → consequence) and rate its severity; the severity sets the target frequency.
                    2. Estimate the initiating event frequency (IEF) from failure data and any enabling condition that must be true at the same time. If several causes lead to the same consequence, work each and add the frequencies.
                    3. Credit each independent protection layer (IPL) with its PFD. A layer that shares a component with the initiating event, or with another credited layer, gets no credit.
                    4. Apply conditional modifiers (occupancy, probability that the event causes harm).
                    5. Compare with the target: RRF = f / target. If RRF > 1, the gap sets the PFD, and so the SIL, of the extra layer.

                    Lecture example: pressure control malfunction 0.1 /yr × high-pressure alarm 0.1 × relief valve 0.01 × occupancy 0.1 = 10−5 /yr against a fatality target of 10−6 /yr → RRF = 10, not acceptable.

                    B2 · Criteria used here (course risk matrix)

                    SeverityTarget risk frequency (/yr)Health and safetyEnvironmentEconomic

                    Likelihood levels by frequency: 5 most likely (~10 /yr), 4 likely (~1), 3 possible (~0.1), 2 rare (~0.01), 1 almost impossible (~0.001); the band boundaries are taken halfway between decades. Risk = severity × likelihood: 1 negligible, 2–6 low, 8–12 medium, 15–20 high, 25 extreme. Target frequencies differ by country (for a fatality about 10−4 to 10−6 /yr). This matrix is stricter than the HAZOP tab's simple ranking bands, which only order the rows.

                    B3 · What counts as an IPL

                    An IPL must be independent of the initiating event and of the other credited layers, specific to the scenario, dependable (its PFD can be justified) and auditable (tested). An alarm needs time: CCPS asks for about 10 minutes between the alarm and the point of no return. Procedures, training, inspection and one-off permissives are safeguards but not IPLs.

                    LayerPFD credited

                    B4 · E-101 LOPA worksheet

                    Independent protection layers
                    Conditional modifiers
                    Initiating eventIEF (/yr)EnablingIPLs credited (struck = ticked but not independent here)ΠPFDCMFrequency (/yr)

                    Part C · Bow-tie

                    A bow-tie is several LOPAs drawn around one top event (the moment control of the hazard is lost). Threats on the left pass prevention (control) barriers; consequences on the right sit behind recovery (mitigation) barriers and conditional modifiers. Escalation factors are conditions that defeat a barrier (a bypass, a blocked impulse line). The top-event frequency is the sum of the threat frequencies times their barrier PFDs. Barrier colours follow the Safety layers tab; grey is a procedure or a conditional modifier. Click a barrier to fail it.

                    Transition operation · startup, shutdown, cleaning, campaigns and load following on E-101

                    Teaching slide deck · why E-101 has transitions, startup and shutdown in order with the reasons, the vacuum after a steam cut, cleaning and storage, set-point campaigns and load following, all run on the model.
                    Open the deck ↗Same folder (offline / GitHub Pages)

                    Follows the course lecture on operating during transitions (Process Operation, with the startup workshop). The Operating windows tab looks at steady states; a transition is the planned transient between an initial and a final condition. Every trend below was produced by running a copy of this simulator's model through the transition with a script (cold startup, shutdown, trip and restart, set-point and load changes); the live plant is not touched. The graded procedures stay on the Exercises tab.

                    1 Transitions · 2 Before startup · 3 Startup · 4 Shutdown and ESD · 5 Vacuum and restart · 6 Cleaning and maintenance · 7 Set-point campaigns · 8 Load following · 9 What makes transitions hard

                    1 · What a transition is, and which ones E-101 has

                    Transitions are planned transient behaviour between different initial and final conditions. They need their own procedures, strategies, process structure and sometimes extra equipment, because the plant was designed for the steady state. E-101 sits between two plants it does not control: the flash-steam header of an upstream plant and the boiler house that takes the heated BFW. Every E-101 transition therefore touches its neighbours.

                    KindWhen it happensOn E-101Part

                    2 · Before startup: the plant is made ready

                    Done before the procedure starts (lecture list, applied to E-101):

                      Extra equipment and features that exist mainly for transitions:

                      ItemWhy a transition needs it

                      3 · Startup from cold: the order and the reasons

                      Initial condition (the cold snapshot the simulator uses): BFW pumps stopped, XV-100 closed and the SIS reset, all controllers in MAN at 0 %, the shell cold and full of air at atmospheric pressure, metal at 25 °C.

                      No.StepWhy this order (analysis)Safety concern

                      How fast may the steam come in? The same script was run from the cold snapshot (pump start, FIC-101 to 100 m³/h, V-104 open, XV-100 opened with FIC-104 in MAN at 5 %) with different ways of raising the FIC-104 output, handing over to cascade when TT-101 reached 66 °C. The model's water-hammer rule is metal below °C while more than kg/h of steam enters (or steam onto a flooded shell).

                      Events in the selected run

                      4 · Shutdown and emergency shutdown: remove the heat first, keep the heat sink last

                      No.StepWhy this order (analysis)Safety concern

                      5 · The shell goes to vacuum when the steam stops, so every restart needs venting

                      Steam that stops flowing keeps condensing on the cold tubes: the shell pressure collapses below atmospheric within seconds. The trap cannot discharge against the return header, and VB-101 opens to let air in (it protects the shell from collapse and lets the condensate drain). The shell is then full of air again, exactly as at a cold start. The restart after an ESD with BFW kept flowing was scripted twice, with the same warm-up and ramp:

                      6 · Cleaning, regeneration and maintenance transitions

                      Heat-transfer surfaces foul and need cleaning; strainers fill; traps, valves and transmitters need maintenance. The lecture's three strategies: parallel equipment (one is cleaned while the other runs), storage (the neighbours run from a tank while the unit is out), or shutdown. On E-101 one side is a utility (flash steam) and the other is the product delivered to the boiler house (BFW), so the questions are different on each side.

                      Cleaning or maintenance on E-101WhyWhat changesHazards and how they are handledStrategy

                      Blocked operation on a bypass

                      While the trap line is out (V-101 and V-102 closed), condensate can only leave through the trap bypass V-103, a hand valve with no steam seal: too little opening and the shell floods, too much and live steam blows through to the return header. This is a temporary, attended operation: an operator stays at the valve, the time is kept short, and the steam loss and hotwell are watched. It is a transition in its own right, with an entry step (line up the bypass, then isolate the trap) and an exit step (trap back in service, then close the bypass).

                      How big must the storage be?

                      E-101 has no parallel exchanger and no buffer of heated BFW. To keep the boilers fed while it is out, either stored BFW covers the outage (holdup time V/F ≥ outage time) or the BFW bypasses the bundle (recommended addition) and the boiler house heats it with its own steam.

                      7 · Set-point campaigns: changing the outlet temperature

                      When the same equipment serves different needs it runs in blocks of steady operation separated by transitions; material made during the transition is off-specification, so transitions should be expedited. Suppose the boiler house asks for a lower BFW temperature (70 → 63 °C) for a period. Off-spec time is counted while TT-101 is more than 1 °C from the new target:

                      What a lower outlet does to the shell pressure and the trap

                      E-101 has a fixed area, so less duty means a lower condensing temperature, and the shell pressure floats down with it. The trap needs a pressure difference to the return header; below a certain outlet the trap cannot pass the condensate, the hotwell rises into the tubes and the flooded area takes over part of the control (a stall). Steady states from the model, cascade in service:

                      8 · Load following: the boiler house sets the BFW rate

                      A supplier that feeds consumers without storage must follow the load in time. E-101 has no tank between it and the boilers: when the boiler house raises its demand, FIC-101 follows and the steam must follow the water. The FIC-101 set point was moved 100 → 120 m³/h at several ramp rates with TIC-101 in cascade:

                      Lecture's industrial practice (steam systems)Same idea on E-101

                      9 · Batch processes, and what makes transitions hard

                      Batch operation (all material at the start) and semi-batch (some added later) never reach a steady state: every batch is a transition, used for small quantities, high purity or long residence times, with storage between batch and continuous sections. E-101 is continuous, so its transitions are the ones above.

                        References: course lecture on operating during transitions and the process startup workshop (Process Operation); T. Marlin, Process Operability class materials; general steam-system practice for heat exchangers (venting of non-condensables, trap selection, vacuum breakers, water-hammer prevention); TEMA practice for exchanger cleaning.

                        Process reliability · how long E-101 delivers hot BFW between outages, and how to make it run longer

                        Teaching slide deck · reliability, failure rate and availability, series, parallel, standby and k-out-of-N structures on E-101, the fouling-driven cleaning interval, inventory, maintenance and life-cycle cost.
                        Open the deck ↗Same folder (offline / GitHub Pages)

                        Follows the course material on reliability (operability in process design, the reliability chapter and its workshop; failure statistics, MTTF/MTBF, series, parallel and k-of-N models, critical items). This tab treats reliability of production: an outage of E-101 costs heat and, if the BFW stops, the boilers' feed. Reliability of safeguards (probability of failure on demand, SIL, layers) is on the LOPA tab. Failure rates marked "course generic" are all-modes values from the course data; everything marked "assumed" is a teaching value, not plant data.

                        1 Definitions · 2 Failure rate and life · 3 Structures · 4 E-101 as a series system · 5 Design for reliability · 6 Fouling and the cleaning interval · 7 Inventory · 8 Maintenance · 9 Life-cycle cost · 10 Steam-heater reliability audit

                        1 · Reliability, availability and why they differ

                        TermDefinitionOn E-101

                        Availability is not reliability. A heater that trips twelve times a year but restarts in fifteen minutes each time has high availability and poor reliability; every trip is a vacuum, an air-filled shell, a vent-and-warm-up restart and a cold spell for the boilers. The course example: three years of the same plant with uptimes 6815, 7612 and 8471 h of 8760 h.

                        2 · Failure rate, the bathtub and the exponential model

                        Failure rate λ(t) = failures per unit time divided by the items still working. Over life it often follows the bathtub: infant mortality (falling λ), chance failures (constant λ), wear-out (rising λ). Most real equipment does not follow the full bathtub (reliability-centred maintenance studies found six patterns, most without wear-out), so the right maintenance depends on the pattern. With constant λ:

                        R(t) = e−λt,   F(t) = 1 − R(t),   MTTF = 1/λ

                        At t = MTTF only 37 % survive (63.2 % have failed). Course example: λ = 0.0001 /h → MTTF 10 000 h; R(5000 h) = e−0.5 = 0.61. The Weibull model R(t) = exp[−(t/η)β] covers all three regions with the shape β:

                        3 · Structures: series, parallel, standby, k out of N

                        A plant is many components joined in structures; the structure sets the system reliability. All formulas assume independent failures (no common cause) and, for standby, perfect switching.

                        StructureWorks whenReliabilityMTTF (identical elements, λ each)E-101 example

                        4 · E-101 as a series system: what stops the hot BFW, and how often

                        For production every element in the chain pump → BFW valve and flow loop → tubes → steam supply and FV-104 → condensate removal → temperature loop → trips must work, so E-101 is a series system: λsys = Σ λi × fi, where fi is the fraction of element i's failures that stop the unit (a spurious trip, lost flow, lost heating). Each outage costs the repair or switching time plus a restart: . Toggle design changes and watch outages, availability and the Pareto.

                        5 · Design for reliability

                        Lecture principleWhat it meansE-101 as builtGap or recommendation

                        "There is no safe side in equipment sizing." An oversized trap cycles hard and wears out; an undersized one floods the shell at low pressure. An oversized pump runs far left of its best-efficiency point and fails on seals and bearings. On E-101 the lesson runs the other way too: FV-104 is sized for design with little margin, so fouling and load both reach its travel limit early (part 6 and the Transition operation tab).

                        6 · Operating for reliability: fouling and the cleaning interval

                        The lecture's trade-off: a short-term gain (running on, pushing a variable toward a constraint) against long-term life. On E-101 the slow killer is scale inside the tubes. As the fouling resistance grows, the controller keeps 70 °C by raising the shell pressure, until FV-104 runs out of travel. The model was run to steady state (owRun, cascade in service) at increasing scale severity; pick the load and the header pressure, set a fouling rate, and read the cleaning interval:

                        7 · Reliability through inventory: TK-101 hold-up

                        A tank between an unreliable unit and the next one lets the next unit keep running while the first is repaired. With the upstream unit's repair time exponentially distributed (mean MTTR) and a hold-up time τ = V/F, the chance that one outage is covered by the tank is 1 − e−τ/MTTR, so Rsys = R2[R1 + (1 − R1)(1 − e−τ/MTTR)]. For E-101 the upstream unit is the water treatment that fills TK-101 (outside the simulator), and unit 2 is E-101 itself, with R2 taken live from part 4.

                        Inventory has a price: tank cost and space, water that must be kept deaerated or chemically treated, and heat lost from stored hot water. The engineer places inventory next to the unreliable unit and sizes it for that unit's repair time; a tank after E-101 would need to hold heated BFW (Transition operation tab, storage calculator).

                        8 · Maintenance for reliability

                        StrategyIdeaE-101 items that suit it

                        9 · Life-cycle cost: how many BFW pumps?

                        Life-cycle costing adds to the usual profitability analysis the costs that reliability changes: maintenance and spares, failure frequency, the cost of each failure (repair, lost production, restart) and the extra equipment for redundancy. The course example asks how many pumps to install. Costs below are assumed teaching values; the restart time comes from the Transition operation tab.

                        Efficiency · where E-101's flash steam goes, and what it is worth to the boiler
