                        1 Efficiency and priorities · 2 Chains multiply · 3 E-101 efficiency now · 4 BFW preheat and the boiler · 5 Venting · 6 Steam traps · 7 Fouling · 8 Pump energy · 9 Push toward the constraint · 10 Energy monitoring
                        Economic basis (assumed teaching values)

                        1 · Efficiency, optimisation and their place among the priorities

                        Efficiency (in operation, the same as optimisation) is good economic performance: the product delivered at the rate and quality needed with less energy, raw material and effluent, and less environmental impact. For energy: efficiency = useful energy output ÷ energy input.

                        For E-101 the useful output is the heat picked up by the BFW, F·cp·(Tout − Tin); the input is the energy the flash steam brings. Four ways to improve it: design with the right capacities (pump, valve, surface); use the existing equipment in the most efficient way (vent, trap, clean tubes); choose a better process structure (recover the flash steam at all, return the condensate); choose the best operating conditions inside the window (part 9).

                        Efficiency is not first: an operator never trades a higher priority for it. Opening the vent wastes steam but protects the surface and the tubes; keeping BFW flowing after a steam trip wastes nothing yet matters more than anything on this tab.

                        PriorityObjectiveOn E-101

                        2 · Chains multiply: flash steam → BFW → boiler fuel

                        Efficiencies in series multiply. The lecture example is electricity: boiler 90 % × turbo-generator 40 % × transmission 90 % = 32.4 %. For E-101 the chain runs the other way and ends in a division: every kilowatt put into the BFW is a kilowatt the boiler does not have to raise from fuel, and the boiler needs 1/ηboiler kW of fuel for each kilowatt it adds to the water. Recovered low-grade steam therefore saves more fuel than its own heat.

                        3 · E-101 efficiency now: direct and indirect method

                        Direct method: η = heat picked up by the BFW ÷ energy brought by the steam, both from meters (FIC-101, TT-101, TI-103 for the water; FIC-104 and PI-100 → Tsat for the steam). Indirect method: η = 100 % − losses, each loss taken from the model's own states (vent steam Wvent, live steam through the trap, bypass or drain Wsl, steam condensed on leaking BFW). Two bases for "energy in": the latent basis Win·λ(Ts), which is what a steam heater is designed to use, and the enthalpy basis Win·(hsteam − hmake-up) above the BFW inlet temperature, which also counts the heat that leaves in the condensate. Both are computed live from the running simulator.

                        4 · The value of BFW preheat to the boiler

                        Each °C of preheat in E-101 is heat the boiler does not have to supply: fuel saved ≈ F·ρ·cp·ΔT ÷ ηboiler. The flow and water properties are the model's; the boiler efficiency and fuel price are the assumed basis above. The CO₂ factor is an assumed natural-gas value.

                        5 · Venting: steam lost against blanketing and the FV-104 margin

                        Gas that does not condense collects at the far end of the shell and blankets tubes; TIC-101 then opens FV-104 and raises the shell pressure to push the same heat through less surface. A vent removes the gas but blows live steam with it. The model runs below (3 h each, so the gas inventory settles) sweep the air vent V-104 from closed to 50 % at four gas loads (share of the fault's full rate), and compare two design alternatives on the P&ID: rev B, a fixed restriction orifice RO-101 around V-104, and rev C, an automatic air vent AAV-101 that opens only when its line runs cool (TI-102). This is a design trade-off, not one right setting: the right answer depends on how much gas the steam carries, and that changes.

                        6 · Steam traps: a failed-open trap, and what a trap survey is worth

                        A trap that fails open passes live steam to the condensate return. TIC-101 does not see it: the outlet stays on set point and FIC-104 simply rises, so the loss appears only in a steam balance or a trap survey. Model runs with ST-101 failing open by different amounts:

                        Across a site the same mechanism repeats at every trap. Survey calculator: steam lost through one failed-open trap by the Napier orifice relation, W = Cd × 51.4 × A[in²] × P[psia] lb/h (assumed discharge coefficient), at the trap's inlet pressure.

                        7 · Fouling: scale inside the tubes

                        Scale adds a resistance in series with the tube-side film, so UA falls and PDI-109 rises. At first nothing is lost on the latent basis: the controller simply raises the shell pressure (and FV-104) to push the same heat through the dirtier surface. The cost is margin, and once FV-104 runs out, outlet shortfall, which the boiler must make up with fuel. Model runs at design flow and header pressure:

                        8 · Pump energy: recycle and throttling against a variable-speed drive

                        P-101A runs at constant speed. FIC-101 sets the flow by throttling FV-101A, and FV-101B opens by the same amount FV-101A closes, so part of the pumped water only goes round the recycle. Both burn pump energy. A variable-speed drive (VSD) could set the flow by speed with FV-101A wide open (affinity laws: flow ∝ speed, head ∝ speed², power ∝ speed³). The hydraulics below solve the model's own pump, valve and tube equations; pump, motor and drive efficiencies and the electricity price are assumed.

                        9 · Best operating conditions: push toward the constraint

                        Many settings do not touch safety or quality but do move the fuel bill; the best value usually sits against a constraint, and how close you can go depends on variability. For E-101 a hotter outlet saves boiler fuel (part 4). Which constraint binds? The temperature limits downstream, or the steam supply through FV-104? Move the set point and the variability and see.

                        Industrial practice: reduce variability first, then move the set point; optimise slowly (a fast optimiser upsets the boiler house), from a model when one exists and from careful plant tests when not; change the alarm limits and the operating window through management of change, never by habit.

                        10 · Energy monitoring: key energy variables for E-101

                        A plant energy dashboard tracks the specific energy consumption against its benchmark and the key energy variables (KEV) that move it.                         1 What an SOP is · 2 Format · 3 SOP register · 4 SOP viewer · 5 Writing rules · 6 Life of an SOP

                        1 · What an SOP is, and which activities need one

                        A standard operating procedure is the written, approved way to carry out one task: the same steps, in the same order, with the same checks, whoever is on shift. It turns the reasons worked out on the other tabs (start-up order, operating window, trips, venting) into actions an operator can follow under pressure.

                        Process safety management requires written procedures for each operating phase (OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119(f)): initial startup, normal operations, temporary operations, emergency shutdown (including who decides and when), emergency operations, normal shutdown, and startup after a turnaround or an emergency shutdown; plus the operating limits with the consequences of deviation and the steps to correct or avoid it, the safety and health considerations (hazards, precautions, exposure control), and the safety systems and their functions. Procedures must be readily available, certified as current each year, and cover safe work practices such as lockout/tagout and line opening.

                        6 · The life of an SOP

                        Draft from the design intent and the hazard studies (HAZID, HAZOP, LOPA) → verify on the simulator (the graded procedures in the Exercises tab run the same steps) → review by operations, process and safety → approve and train → use, with every deviation reported → review after any change (management of change), after an incident or near miss, and at the fixed interval (certified annually under PSM), then revise and re-issue.

                        References: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119(f) Operating procedures and (j) mechanical integrity; OSHA 29 CFR 1910.147 Control of hazardous energy (lockout/tagout); CCPS, Guidelines for Writing Effective Operating and Maintenance Procedures; Thai Department of Industrial Works notification on process safety management.
